This guide reviews 6 months of incidents, sets out a 4-pillar incident response playbook, and shows it in practice through Fireworks AI and Klue. The post Not If, But How: Responding to Security Incidents in the Age of AI Attackers appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Attackers now have powerful AI on their side. AI agents can scan, plan and run intrusions at machine speed, and they improve every month. The result is more attacks, more often and at global scale. In that environment, more companies will face a security incident at some point. What separates them is how they respond. Machine-speed threats call for a modern playbook with 4 pillars. Detect and contain automatically. Communicate fast and securely. Eradicate thoroughly. Keep shrinking the blast radius. This article shows the trend through 6 months of incidents. It then looks at a few companies, with Fireworks AI as a model of mature, structurally sound response. TL;DR The trend: AI-powered attackers are driving more frequent attacks at global scale. The evidence: Several AI platforms disclosed security incidents between May and November 2026. Pillar 1: Detect and contain automatically. Human-speed shutdowns are too slow. Pillar 2: Communicate fast and securely, over out-of-band channels. Pillar 3: Eradicate thoroughly, with outside forensic experts. Pillar 4: Keep shrinking the blast radius. Data that is never stored cannot be stolen. Case studies: Fireworks AI and Klue show these pillars in practice. Why are attacks becoming more frequent? AI has changed the economics of attacking. Tasks that took skilled people days can now be delegated to agents. In November, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said AI misuse had reached a “critical inflection point” . They report that attackers use AI to shorten timelines and run multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. CrowdStrike reported that 1 group used AI agents against more than 200 organizations in 11 days . Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 found attacks moving about 4 times faster than a year earlier. The shift started earlier. In 2025, Anthropic disrupted a campaign where AI did 80 to 90% of tactical work with little human input. The tools keep improving, so the pace will keep rising. AI infrastructure is an especially attractive target, because AI access itself has value. The last 6 months show what that looks like. What was disclosed in the last 6 months? Incidents appeared across every layer of the AI stack. Together they show how broad the activity has become. May: package registries. On May 10 and 11, the “Mini Shai-Hulud” campaign altered about 170 npm packages and some PyPI libraries . Affected projects included AI SDKs from Mistral AI and Guardrails AI. The NHS cyber alert lists the specific versions to avoid. June: SaaS integrations. Klue, a market intelligence platform, disclosed misuse of OAuth tokens it held for customers. See case study 2. August: self-hosted AI gateways. Microsoft described intrusions into exposed, unpatched LiteLLM, RAGFlow and Kestra deployments. Fixed versions exist for all 3 tools . CISA had listed the LiteLLM flaw as known exploited on June 8. September: evaluation environments. Anthropic’s September threat report described attempts to obtain AI keys through software vendors. The Cloud Security Alliance summarized it . In 1 case, instructions were injected into a vendor’s automated evaluation sandbox. October and early November: developer platforms. At least 9 AI developer and hosting platforms disclosed incidents involving stored customer secrets in October. Wiz’s tracker later listed further disclosures, for 16 platforms in total. A tampered LiteLLM release, version 1.107.0, was also identified , and users were told to roll back. November: shared web vendors. On November 16, an attacker abused a flaw in Optimizely’s account signup flow to inject code into customer projects, reaching 178 organizations’ websites, according to Report URI, including HSBC, Salesforce, the BBC and Ledger. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses and skimmed payment forms; Optimizely removed the payload and fixed the flaw. Hudson Rock traced similar code through three other web services, beginning November 13. It is the same concentration pattern, one layer below the AI stack. Several October entries rely on compilations by Wiz and Helix rather than primary vendor disclosures. What do these incidents have in common? There was no single vulnerability. According to the Cloud Security Alliance, entry points varied . The common target was stored environment variables, often holding AI provider API keys. AI keys carry real value, which explains the interest. CSA, citing Anthropic, notes that a key can be resold, used for compute or used as cover . Wiz estimated that misuse of 2 keys from these incidents exceeded $100,000 at list price . That is why spending caps matter. Concentration is the other shared factor. A platform that stores secrets for many customers naturally draws attention. CSA describes this as the platform-chain pattern . What does a modern incident response playbook look like? No company can promise it will never be breached. Every company can control how it responds. Against attackers that move at machine speed, that response rests on 4 pillars. 1. Detect and contain automatically: A human-speed shutdown is no longer enough. An AI-driven intruder can move between systems in minutes. Mature teams wire detection directly to containment.
